This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.

L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference

sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,

oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Pethidine, a 4-phenylpiperidine opioid structurally related to the query's fentanyl-like piperidine amide, showed absolute oral bioavailability of 0.80 ± 0.15 in cirrhotic patients, supporting F ≥ 20%.
Encainide, a piperidine-containing anilide, showed oral bioavailability of 76–78% in cirrhotic patients, supporting high F for piperidine amide-type drugs.
Meptazinol, an opioid, had absolute bioavailability of 27.9 ± 5.3% in cirrhosis, still above the 20% threshold.
Ziprasidone, a heteroaryl piperazine with a thiophene-like benzisothiazole, had absolute bioavailability of approximately 59–60% when given with a high-fat meal.
Thiophene-containing drugs tenidap, suprofen, and R406 had absolute bioavailability values of 85%, 92.2%, and 55%, respectively, all supporting F ≥ 20%.
Additional positive oral bioavailability records include SAHA 43% fasted, FK788 55%, and PEMA at least 80%, none of which suggest F < 20%.

evidence_gaps: No direct oral bioavailability measurement exists for the query molecule itself.
Most relevant records are from cirrhosis or fed/fasted conditions, while the query condition is unspecified; absolute F may differ in a healthy, fasted setting.
No experimental solubility, permeability, or first-pass metabolism data are available for the query.
Structural differences from the closest contexts, especially the methoxymethyl and thiophene substituents, could alter metabolic clearance and absorption.
content.decision_summary: All L1 gold records show absolute oral bioavailability at or above 27.9%, with most values above 50%, and the most transferable contexts (pethidine, encainide, meptazinol, ziprasidone, and thiophene-containing drugs) support F ≥ 20% for this fentanyl-like piperidine amide. No affirmative threshold-relevant evidence supports F < 20%, so the prediction is high with moderate confidence.
